headline: Bitcoin slides as hot CPI data revives Fed rate-hike fears and ETF outflows mount
summary: October's inflation reading came in hotter than expected — CPI up 0.4% for the month — and traders quickly repriced the odds of a December Fed rate hike, sending Bitcoin down 0.46% to $74,093 and pulling most of the top 20 lower. The pressure wasn't just macro: spot Bitcoin ETFs saw accelerating outflows at the same time miner MARA disclosed it sold nearly 13,600 BTC over six weeks and plans to keep selling. Ethereum fell 2.1%, Solana dropped 3.4%, and the Fear & Greed index sits at 32 — squarely in fear territory. The one bright spot was Gram, the Telegram-native token, which gained 4.5% after its wallet product rebranded and launched as a standalone trading app.

winners.name: Gram (prev. Toncoin)
winners.catalyst: The Telegram-native crypto wallet rebranded to Walt and launched as a standalone trading app, driving renewed attention to the Gram ecosystem and its user base. This product independence narrative boosted sentiment around the token.

losers.name: Rain
losers.catalyst: No specific catalyst identified; the move appears technical amid a broad risk-off session driven by hotter-than-expected CPI data.

whyItMoved:
The day's main driver was a hotter-than-expected US inflation report. October CPI rose 0.4% month-over-month, above forecasts, and the core rate — which strips out food and energy — came in at 0.3%. That was enough to shift market expectations toward a December Fed rate hike, which tends to be negative for risk assets including crypto. Bitcoin fell 0.46% to $74,093, but the macro print was only part of the story.

Two supply-side forces compounded the pressure on Bitcoin specifically. First, spot Bitcoin ETFs saw accelerating outflows — institutional money exiting the funds that have been a key demand driver since their January 2024 launch. Second, mining company MARA disclosed it sold 13,597 BTC — roughly $1.1 billion worth — over the past six weeks and signaled it plans to continue. That combination of ETF redemptions and miner liquidation created meaningful selling pressure at a moment when the macro backdrop was already unfavorable.

Notably, Bitcoin declined even as US equities rebounded on the day, a divergence that underscores how much of BTC's recent support has come from ETF-driven institutional flows rather than broad risk appetite. When those flows reverse, Bitcoin loses the cushion that had been keeping it elevated relative to other risk assets.

Ethereum fell 2.1% to $2,076, Solana dropped 3.4% to $84.16, and Monero slid 8.1% — the sharpest decline among the top 15 tracked assets. The Fear & Greed index at 32 reflects the cautious tone across the market.
worthKnowing: Coinbase, Kalshi, and Payward (Kraken's parent) filed briefs backing the CFTC in a lawsuit over single-stock perpetual futures — a case that could define where the regulatory line sits between crypto derivatives and traditional finance.
Gram's wallet product, previously embedded inside Telegram, rebranded to Walt and launched as a standalone trading app, expanding its reach beyond Telegram's user base.
Monero fell 8.1% on the day with no clear catalyst identified — the move stands out given the broader market's relatively contained losses.
